question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer:
No. When a permanent phases in, it does not trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities. Rule [702.26d] states explicitly: "The phasing event doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones or control... Zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out." Phasing in (or out) is not a zone change at all — the permanent was never treated as having left the battlefield in a rules sense, even though it was treated as though it weren't on the battlefield while phased out ([702.26d]). Rule [702.26c] confirms that phasing in simply changes the permanent's status back to "phased in," and the game again treats it as existing — it doesn't re-enter as a new object.

By contrast, true zone-change triggers such as "When [this] enters, ..." (an enters-the-battlefield trigger, [603.6a]) or "When [this] leaves the battlefield, ..." (a leaves-the-battlefield trigger, [603.6c]) only fire on actual movement between zones, and phasing is specifically carved out as not being such a movement. Similarly, [702.26j] notes that attach/unattach triggers don't fire from phasing either — this is the same underlying principle: phasing bypasses zone-change and state-change triggers generally.

This holds true whether the phasing happens via the normal untap-step turn-based action ([502.1], [703.4a], [702.26a]) or via a one-shot "phases out until" effect ([610.4], [610.4a], [610.4c]) — in every case, the permanent phasing in does not generate an ETB trigger, and any Aura/Equipment/Fortification that reattaches ([702.26i]) likewise doesn't retrigger attach-based abilities.

This answer applies the same way in both two-player and multiplayer games — the no-ETB-trigger rule for phasing ([702.26d]) isn't conditioned on player count. The only multiplayer-specific wrinkle noted in the rules is [702.26n], which addresses when a permanent that phased out under a player who then left the game will eventually phase in (during the next untap step after that departed player's next turn would have begun) — but even then, phasing in still doesn't trigger ETB abilities, since [702.26d] still applies.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, the deathtouch ability lets its controller treat any nonzero amount of damage assigned to each blocking creature as "lethal damage" for trample-assignment purposes, so only 1 damage per blocker needs to be assigned to satisfy trample's lethal-damage requirement, and the rest can be sent to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle.

Here's why: Trample (a static ability, rule [702.19a]) requires its controller to first assign lethal damage to all blocking creatures before assigning any excess damage to the defending player/planeswalker/battle, per rule [702.19b]. Rule [702.19b] says that when checking for "assigned lethal damage," you take into account damage already marked and damage from other sources being assigned simultaneously, but not abilities/effects that would change how much damage is actually dealt. Deathtouch, however, changes what counts as lethal, not how much damage is dealt: rule [702.2c] states that any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for determining whether excess damage is being dealt. So a creature with trample and deathtouch can legally assign just 1 damage to a blocking creature (satisfying the lethal-damage requirement) and route all remaining damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking.

This also matches rule [120.4a], which defines "excess damage" for a creature receiving deathtouch damage as anything above 1 damage, confirming that only 1 point is needed to be lethal in this context.

If the attacker instead has trample over planeswalkers and deathtouch, and is attacking a planeswalker, the same logic applies to blockers (1 damage each is enough), but the creature still must assign damage at least equal to the planeswalker's loyalty to the planeswalker itself before any further excess can go to that planeswalker's controller, per rule [702.19c] — deathtouch doesn't reduce the loyalty threshold, since a planeswalker's toughness/loyalty isn't affected by the deathtouch rule (which only concerns creatures, per [702.2b]/[704.5h]).

A few supporting notes: deathtouch functions regardless of what zone the source deals damage from and even if it's no longer where you'd expect (rules [702.2d] and [702.2e], using last known information), and multiple instances of either deathtouch or trample on the same creature are redundant (rules [702.2f] and [702.19g]).

One timing note: this all assumes a normal combat damage step where blockers haven't already been dealt damage or removed from combat. If a blocking creature had already taken lethal damage earlier (e.g., from a spell) or was removed from combat before damage assignment, the trample/deathtouch math would be based on the state at the moment of assignment, per [702.19b] and [506.4c] — I'm assuming no such prior damage or removal here.

When checking for assigned lethal damage, take into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other creatures that’s being assigned during the same combat damage step, but not any abilities or effects that might change the amount of damage that’s actually dealt. The attacking creature’s controller need not assign lethal damage to all those blocking creatures but in that case can’t assign any damage to the player or planeswalker it’s attacking. question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer:
Yes—Storm is a triggered ability, and like other triggered abilities on the stack, it can be countered, but only by an effect that specifically says it counters abilities (not by something that only counters spells).

Storm is defined as "a triggered ability that functions on the stack. 'Storm' means 'When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn...'" [Storm], [702.40a]. Since it's a triggered ability rather than a spell, rule [113.9] applies: "Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, and therefore can't be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities." So a card like Counterspell (which counters a spell) can't stop the Storm trigger, but something worded to counter a triggered ability, or a Ward-style ability that counters abilities [Ward], could counter it.

Once the storm trigger has triggered, it's put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3], [113.3c], and it stays there until it's countered, resolves, or otherwise leaves the stack. If a spell has multiple instances of storm, each one triggers—and therefore could potentially be countered—separately [702.40b].

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer:
No. A card with a hybrid mana symbol (like {R/G}) is considered to be *both* of the colors in that symbol for color-identity purposes, even though you only need one of the two colors to actually pay it. Under rule [202.2d], "An object with one or more hybrid mana symbols ... in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols," and [107.4e] confirms "A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors." Since Commander deckbuilding legality (rule [903.5c]) requires that *every* color in a card's color identity be found in the commander's color identity, a card containing a hybrid symbol such as {R/G} has both red and green in its color identity (per the color-identity definition in [903.4]) and therefore cannot be included in a deck whose commander's color identity is only red or only green -- you need a commander whose color identity includes *both* colors of that hybrid symbol.

This applies regardless of the fact that you can pay a hybrid cost with mana of just one of the two colors ([118.13], [107.4e], [106.8]) -- paying the cost with one color doesn't change what the card's color identity is; that's fixed by the printed symbol itself, not by how it's ultimately paid.

So: if your commander (e.g., a mono-red commander) only has red in its color identity, you cannot include a card whose mana cost or rules text contains a red/green hybrid symbol like {R/G}, {R/W}, etc., because that card's color identity includes green (or white) as well, which isn't in your commander's color identity.

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer: No. You cannot respond to anything happening in the untap step, because no player receives priority during that step at all [502.4][117.3a]. Since no one has priority, no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated during the untap step [502.4]. The untap step's turn-based actions (permanents phasing out/in per rule 703.4a/702.26a, the day/night check per rule 703.4b/502.2, and untapping permanents per rule 502.3/703.4c) all happen automatically without using the stack, and the step simply ends once those actions are complete [500.3]. If something triggers during the untap step (for example, an ability that would trigger off a permanent phasing in or out), it doesn't resolve immediately - it's held and put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which is normally at the start of the upkeep step, once triggered abilities are placed on the stack and the active player receives priority [502.4][503.1][503.1a]. This holds true whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since the 'no priority during untap' rule doesn't depend on how many players are at the table - it's an absolute rule about that step [117.3a][502.4]. Also note rule 500.12: no game events occur between steps, phases, or turns, reinforcing that there's no window to act there either.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer:
Yes. A creature remains an "attacking creature" until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever happens first (see the Attacking Creature definition). The end of combat step is still part of the combat phase - it's the fifth and final step of that phase - so any creature that was declared as an attacker (or put onto the battlefield attacking) and hasn't otherwise been removed from combat is still an attacking creature throughout the end of combat step, including when "at end of combat" triggered abilities go off as that step begins [511.2]. It only stops being an attacking creature once the end of combat step ends, because that's when the combat phase itself ends and rule [511.3] causes all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers to be removed from combat. Note that a creature can also lose attacking-creature status earlier, before the end of combat step, if it's removed from combat for some other reason (leaving the battlefield, changing controllers, phasing out, being specifically removed from combat, etc., per [506.4]) - but absent such an event, it stays an attacking creature all the way through the end of combat step.

This all assumes normal combat proceeding through its steps. If some effect ends the combat phase early (as Mandate of Peace does), the end of combat step itself is skipped entirely and creatures are removed from combat at that point instead [724.2d].

question: Do you cast lands?
answer:
No. You never cast a land card as a spell — you play it. Playing a land means putting it onto the battlefield directly from your hand (or another zone) as a special action; it never uses the stack, so it isn't a spell or ability and can't be countered or responded to [305.1] [701.18a] [116.2a]. Casting, by contrast, is how you put a spell onto the stack, and rule [601.1a] and the glossary entry for 'Play' confirm that the term 'playing a card' specifically covers two distinct things: playing a card as a land, or casting a card as a spell — 'whichever is appropriate' [601.1a] [701.18b]. Because lands aren't cast, they also have no mana cost to pay — mana costs apply to spells, and land cards normally have none, representing an unpayable cost, while rule [202.1b] separately notes that lands are simply played without paying any cost at all.

If a card is both a land and another type (e.g., an artifact land), it still can only be played as a land, never cast as a spell, even though it also has the other card type's characteristics [300.2a] [305.9] [Artifact Land].

Mechanically, you play a land if you have priority, it's a main phase of your turn, the stack is empty, and you haven't already used up your allowed land plays for the turn (normally one, though continuous effects can increase this) [305.1] [305.2] [305.2b] [116.2a]. You can only do this on your own turn — an effect can't let you play a land on someone else's turn [305.3]. This is a special action, not a turn-based or state-based action, and it doesn't go on the stack [116.1] [116.2a]. Note that if an effect instead 'puts' a land onto the battlefield, that's different from 'playing' it and doesn't use up your land-play for the turn [305.4].

This holds the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — none of the rules governing playing lands (priority, main phase, empty stack, one land per turn by default) differ based on player count.

question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer:
Yes — you (or another player, if some effect lets them) can sacrifice the evoked creature to a *different* ability or spell while the evoke triggered ability is still on the stack, before that trigger resolves.

Here's why. Evoke (rule [702.74a]) gives the permanent two things: an alternative cost you pay to cast it, and a triggered ability that reads "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it." That sacrifice instruction is not paid when the creature is cast — it's paid when the triggered ability itself resolves. Like any other triggered ability, it sits on the stack for a time before it resolves, and during that window a player can respond with another spell or ability — for example, a separate sacrifice outlet — that sacrifices the evoked creature for its own cost or effect.

Under rule [118.10], "each payment of a cost applies to only one spell, ability, or effect," so sacrificing the creature to pay for some other ability's cost is a distinct action from the evoke trigger's own sacrifice instruction — it doesn't satisfy the evoke ability, it just happens to remove the same creature from the battlefield first.

If you do this, once the evoke triggered ability actually resolves, the creature is no longer on the battlefield, so "its controller sacrifices it" can't be carried out — you can't sacrifice a permanent that isn't there. Per the general principle in rule [608.2d] that a player can't choose an illegal or impossible option when applying an effect's instructions, the evoke trigger simply does nothing at that point; the creature is already gone via the other sacrifice, so there's no double sacrifice and no extra effect.

Note this assumes the sacrifice happens in response to the evoke trigger while it's still on the stack (i.e., before it resolves), which is the timing your question specifies. If instead the creature were sacrificed only after the evoke trigger had already resolved and sacrificed it, there'd be nothing left to sacrifice a second time anyway, since the creature would already be in the graveyard.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. "Loses all abilities" removes every kind of ability the object has, including keyword abilities. A keyword ability is just a shorthand name for a full set of rules text or a rule for that ability [702.1], and rule [702.1d] confirms that an object "with" a keyword ability is treated the same as an object "with a [keyword] ability" for the purposes of ability-referencing effects — in other words, keyword abilities are abilities like any other. Rule [113.10]/[113.10b] states that an effect removing an ability removes *all instances* of that ability, and "loses all abilities" is simply the broadest version of an ability-removing effect, so it strips keyword abilities, activated abilities, triggered abilities, and static abilities alike, leaving the object with none of them.

A good illustration is the example given for zone-change triggers: if an effect says "All creatures lose all abilities" and a creature with an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability enters the battlefield, that creature loses its abilities the instant it enters, so the triggered ability never actually triggers [603.6b]/[603.6d]. That shows the loss-of-abilities effect reaching a keyword or named triggered ability, not just generic static abilities.

One caveat: a characteristic-defining ability (a static ability that sets or overrides a printed characteristic like power/toughness, e.g. "Power and toughness are each equal to the number of lands you control") still counts as an ability under rule [604.3], so a "loses all abilities" effect would strip that too, reverting the object to its printed/copied characteristics — this is worth flagging if the card in question relies on such an ability for its stats.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. Having a maximum hand size doesn't stop you from drawing cards - it only comes into play during your cleanup step, when you must discard down to that number if you're over it. There's no rule that prevents you from drawing cards, or that reduces the number of cards you draw, just because you're at or above your maximum hand size at some other point in the turn.

Specifically, rule [402.2] says a player may have any number of cards in hand, but as part of their cleanup step they must discard excess cards down to the maximum hand size (normally seven). Rule [514.1] and [703.4n] confirm this discard is a turn-based action that happens immediately after the cleanup step begins, checking whether the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size. So you can freely draw cards - via your normal draw step, spells, abilities, etc. - even while already at seven cards (or whatever your maximum is); you'll simply have to discard down to your maximum size later, during your own cleanup step, if you're still over the limit at that time and you're the active player.

One wrinkle: if your maximum hand size has been modified - for example by a vanguard card's hand modifier as in rule [902.5b], which can set your maximum to six - the same principle applies, just with that adjusted number instead of seven.

question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
answer:
A planeswalker with 0 loyalty counters is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action; loyalty can't actually go below 0 because it's defined as "the number of loyalty counters on it," and you simply can't have a negative number of counters on a permanent.

Here's the detail: loyalty is a characteristic unique to planeswalkers, and for a planeswalker on the battlefield, its loyalty equals the number of loyalty counters currently on it [306.5c]. Loyalty counters are removed by damage (each point of damage dealt to a planeswalker removes one loyalty counter instead of being marked as damage) [120.3c] [306.8], and by the planeswalker's own [-N] loyalty abilities [107.7]. If enough loyalty counters are removed to bring the total to 0, or if some effect otherwise leaves a planeswalker with 0 loyalty counters, the game state-based action check (rule 704) finds that a planeswalker has loyalty 0 and puts it into its owner's graveyard [704.5i] [306.9] [122.1e]. State-based actions like this don't use the stack — they happen automatically the moment a player would receive priority, with no opportunity for anyone to respond [704.1].

Since "loyalty" is literally just a count of counters on the permanent, there's no mechanism for it to go below 0 — if a removal or damage effect would remove more counters than are present, the planeswalker just ends up at 0 counters (loyalty 0), which then triggers the same state-based action and sends it to the graveyard. So practically, "0 or less loyalty" and "exactly 0 loyalty" describe the same real game state.

This is analogous to a player's life total: a player with 0 or less life loses the game the next time a player would receive priority, also via a state-based action [104.3b] [119.6] — but for planeswalkers the corresponding state-based action is going to the graveyard, not causing a player to lose (unless that planeswalker's controller/owner has some other effect tied to it).

This rule and its enforcement are the same regardless of whether the game has two players or more than two — nothing in these rules ties the planeswalker-loyalty state-based action to the number of players.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer:
No. "Dies" is a defined game term that applies only to creatures and planeswalkers: a creature or planeswalker "dies" if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield (rule 700.4, and the "Dies" reminder rule). A non-creature artifact (an artifact that is not also a creature) is neither a creature nor a planeswalker, so when it goes from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard, that event is simply described as being "put into the graveyard" — it is not correctly described as "dying," even in casual conversation, if you're using the rules-precise sense of the term.

If the artifact is an artifact creature (an object with both the artifact and creature types), it does die when put into the graveyard from the battlefield, because such an object combines the aspects of both card types (rule 300.2) and is a creature for rules purposes, including the "dies" trigger condition.

Separately, note that being put into the graveyard is not the same as being "destroyed." A permanent (including a non-creature artifact) is only "destroyed" if an effect uses the word "destroy" or if it's removed via the lethal-damage/deathtouch state-based actions in rule 704.5g/704.5h — and those state-based actions only ever apply to creatures, since non-creature permanents have no power or toughness (rule 208.3) and can't take damage in the toughness-comparison sense the same way. A non-creature artifact can still leave the battlefield to the graveyard through sacrifice, a "put into graveyard" effect, or destruction, but none of those events is termed "dying" unless the object is also a creature.

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You don't lose the instant you try to draw—you lose the game the next time any player would receive priority. Attempting to draw a card from an empty library doesn't immediately end the game; instead, rule [704.5b] makes this a state-based action: if a player has attempted to draw from an empty library since the last state-based action check, that player loses the game. Rule [121.4] confirms the timing: the loss happens "the next time a player would receive priority," not the moment the draw is attempted. So there can be a brief window (e.g., mid-resolution of a spell or ability) where you've already failed to draw but haven't lost yet, until the game checks state-based actions again.

If an effect requires you to draw more cards than remain in your library (e.g., 'draw three' but only one card is left), rule [104.3c] says you draw as many as you can (the remaining cards) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority — same state-based-action mechanism.

A few related wrinkles: if an effect *replaces* a card draw, that replacement effect still applies even though your library is empty, per rules [121.6a] and [614.11] — so you don't necessarily lose if something is replacing the draw itself. Also, if an effect merely offers you the *choice* to draw (rather than mandating it), rule [121.3] lets you choose to do so even with an empty library, and rule [121.3a] extends this even when the player being offered the choice isn't the one who'd actually draw.

This works the same regardless of how many players are in the game — rule [704.1] states state-based actions are checked and applied automatically for any game, and losing via [704.5b] isn't dependent on being a two-player game. In a multiplayer game, if you lose this way, you're simply removed from the game (per the normal multiplayer elimination process) while the remaining players continue; the empty-library rule itself doesn't change based on player count.

Note on timing: I'm assuming the draw attempt happens and then the very next priority-passing check applies the loss — if instead multiple triggered abilities or replacement effects are stacked up before that check, the loss is still delayed until priority would next be given, per [121.4].

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
Combat has five steps, always in this order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. If no creatures are declared as attackers (and none are put onto the battlefield attacking), the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped entirely [506.1].

As the defending player, here's when you get priority in each step:

- Beginning of combat step: In a two-player game, the active player is automatically the attacking player and you (the nonactive player) are automatically the defending player, with no turn-based choice needed [506.2, 506.2a]. In a multiplayer game where opponents don't all automatically become defending players, the active player must choose one opponent as a turn-based action to become the defending player before anyone gets priority [507.1, 703.4h]. Either way, after that turn-based action (if any) resolves, priority is available during the step.

- Declare blockers step: You, the defending player, declare blockers as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [509.1, 703.4j]. You don't get to respond with instants/abilities *during* the act of declaring blockers itself; priority becomes available only after that turn-based action is complete.

- Combat damage step: Damage assignment (who deals damage to what) is also a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack — the active player announces attacking creatures' damage assignments, then you as defending player announce blocking creatures' damage assignments [510.1, 703.4k]. (In a multiplayer game, damage is assigned in APNAP — active-player, then non-active-players — order [802.5].) Critically, once damage is assigned, it's all dealt simultaneously as a further turn-based action, and no player — including you — gets a chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the assignment and the dealing of damage [510.2]. Priority only becomes available after damage has actually been dealt.

- End of combat step: This step has no turn-based actions at all. As soon as it begins, the active player gets priority first [511.1]. The rules provided don't spell out the exact order priority rotates through after that point beyond the active player receiving it first, but as defending player you would receive priority after the active player passes.

One gap to flag: the rules given explicitly state that the active player gets priority first only for the end of combat step [511.1]. For the beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, and combat damage steps, the provided rules don't restate who receives priority first — they only describe the turn-based actions and note that priority exists as a general system [117.1]. So while I can tell you when priority windows open and close relative to those turn-based actions, I can't cite a specific provided rule confirming you'd be second in line for priority in those earlier steps versus the active player being first.

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer:
No. A mana ability never uses the stack, so there is no window to respond to it in the sense described by rule 117.7 (casting a spell or activating an ability while something is already on the stack). Rule 605.3b states that an activated mana ability "doesn't go on the stack, so it can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated." Rule 605.4a says the same thing about triggered mana abilities: they resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered them, without waiting for priority. Rule 405.6c reinforces this: mana abilities resolve immediately, and if a player had priority before activating one, they simply get priority back after it resolves - there's no stack object sitting there for anyone to respond to.

What you *can* do is activate other mana abilities (or take other actions) at essentially the same moment, since rule 605.3a lets a player activate a mana ability whenever they have priority, or whenever they're casting a spell, activating an ability, or a rule/effect calls for a mana payment - even mid-resolution of something else. But that's not "responding" in the stack sense; it's just another immediate, non-stack action happening around the same time. Once you've begun activating a particular mana ability, that same ability can't be activated again until it resolves (605.3c), but this doesn't create a response window for opponents or anyone else.

This holds the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game - nothing about the stack-avoidance of mana abilities changes with player count.

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer:
No. Paying a cost is not itself a stack action, so there's no window to respond to it. Casting a spell or activating an activated ability involves paying its cost as one of the steps of putting that spell or ability onto the stack (rule 602.1 defines an activated ability as "[Cost]: [Effect]", and 118.1–118.2 describe carrying out the cost's instructions as part of that process); no player gets priority in the middle of that process, so nothing can be done in response to the act of paying itself. The same is true for turn-based actions like declaring attackers or declaring blockers, which explicitly "don't use the stack" (508.1j, 509.1e, 509.1f) — you pay any required costs as part of that single turn-based action, with no opportunity for opponents to respond in between.

What you *can* do is respond after the spell or ability has been fully cast or activated (cost paid, object now on the stack) — at that point players receive priority and may respond to the resulting spell or ability itself, not to the cost payment. If a player is unable to complete paying a cost partway through, rule 733.1 says the entire action is reversed as an illegal action rather than something an opponent "responds" to.

This holds the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — none of the rules on cost payment or the declare-attackers/blockers steps change based on player count; multiplayer only changes things like who is a defending player or what happens if a player has left the game (not cited here since not relevant to this question).

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
The layer system is the procedure the game uses to determine, in order, how continuous effects apply to an object's characteristics (rule [Layer]). Per rule [613.1], the game starts with an object's 'actual' values (for a card, its printed values; for a token or copy, the values defined by the effect that created it), and then applies every applicable continuous effect in a fixed sequence of layers. The layers given in the provided rules are: Layer 1 – rules and effects that modify copiable values ([613.1a]), which itself has sublayers, with Layer 1a covering copy effects and merging with permanents such as via mutate ([613.2], [613.2a], [707.1], [730.1]); Layer 3 – text-changing effects ([613.1c], [612.1]); Layer 4 – type-changing effects, i.e. changes to card type, subtype, and/or supertype ([613.1d]); Layer 5 – color-changing effects ([613.1e]); and Layer 7 – power/toughness effects, which also has its own sublayers applied in order ([613.4]).

Within each layer or sublayer, effects are normally applied in timestamp order—the effect with the earlier timestamp goes first ([613.7])—unless a dependency exists between two effects in that same layer/sublayer, in which case dependency overrides timestamp order ([613.8], [Dependency]).

A single effect can have parts that belong to different layers; each part is applied in its own appropriate layer, and once an effect starts applying to a set of objects it keeps applying to that same set in later layers even if its source is removed in between ([613.6]). For example, 'gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice' applies its color change in Layer 5 and its +1/+1 in Layer 7 (sublayer c); Act of Treason's 'gain control... it gains haste' applies control-change in Layer 2 (mentioned only via example, not separately defined here) and haste in Layer 6.

All of this happens continually and automatically as the game state changes, and the resulting characteristic changes are instantaneous ([613.5]). The rules also give a worked example: Honor of the Pure grants white creatures +1/+1; if a black creature is turned white by a Layer 5 effect, it then picks up Honor of the Pure's +1/+1 in Layer 7c, and if later turned red, it loses that bonus again ([613.5]).

Note: the provided rules do not include the full list/definitions of Layers 2 and 6 (control-changing and ability-adding effects, referenced only in examples), or the specific sublayers of Layer 7, so I can't give you the complete official layer list beyond what's cited here.

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
The legend rule is a state-based action: if a player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the exact same name, that player must choose one of them to keep, and all the others are put into their owners' graveyards. This applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype, which includes legendary creatures, legendary planeswalkers (including older planeswalkers that received errata to become legendary per rule 306.4), legendary artifacts, and legendary lands.

Key points on how it works:
- It's a state-based action, so it's checked continuously by the game rules (rule 704.5j) rather than needing a spell or ability to trigger it. Whenever the game state has a player controlling two or more legendary permanents with the same name, this action fires the next time state-based actions are checked, before any player gets priority.
- The rule cares about the permanents' names being identical, not about the cards being physically the same card or having the same abilities at the time - if two objects have the same name and both have the legendary supertype, and the same player controls both, the rule applies.
- The affected player - not any other player - chooses which one of the duplicate legendary permanents to keep; the rest go to their owners' graveyards (note: each goes to its own owner's graveyard, which matters if permanents changed control).
- The legendary supertype itself is independent of card type; a permanent's other characteristics can change without removing its legendary status, and gaining/losing other supertypes doesn't affect whether it's still legendary.
- Legendary tokens (created via effects that say "create [name], a legendary...") are also subject to the rule, since they're simply tokens with the legendary supertype and the given name.

This differs from the casting restriction on legendary instants/sorceries (rule 205.4e), which stops a player from casting such a spell unless they control a legendary creature or planeswalker - that's a separate rule and doesn't involve the legend rule's "choose one, graveyard the rest" mechanic.

This works the same regardless of how many players are in the game - the legend rule only cares about how many legendary permanents with the same name a single player controls, not about opponents or other players' boards, so it applies identically in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature doesn't die the instant the damage is marked; it dies the next time state-based actions are checked, which happens automatically before any player would receive priority. Damage dealt to a creature is marked on it (rule 302.7, 120.3e). A creature with toughness greater than 0 that has damage marked on it greater than or equal to its toughness has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action (rules 704.5g, 302.7, 120.6). Rule 120.5 makes clear that the damage itself, or its source, does not destroy the creature directly - state-based actions do the destroying.

State-based actions don't use the stack (704.1) and are checked and performed automatically every time a player would receive priority - before that player actually gets priority (117.5, 117.2d). So in practice, once lethal damage is marked (for example, right after combat damage is dealt simultaneously to all creatures per rule 703.4m, or right after a damage-dealing spell/ability finishes resolving), the game checks state-based actions before anyone can act, and your creature is destroyed and put into its owner's graveyard at that point - not later in the turn, and not waiting for the cleanup step. (The damage itself would stay marked on the creature until cleanup per rule 120.6/514.2 only if the creature *survives*, e.g., if the damage weren't lethal.)

One timing note: if the damage was dealt by a source with deathtouch, the creature is destroyed as a state-based action even if the damage isn't literally lethal by the toughness math, per rule 702.2b/704.5h - same 'checked before priority' timing applies.

This answer assumes a normal priority-based sequence; the only listed exception is if an effect is ending the turn, in which case state-based actions are still checked as part of that special turn-ending sequence (724.1c) rather than through the normal priority process, but the destruction still happens as a state-based action at that check.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
By default, no — a commander is normally cast from the command zone, not from exile. Rule [903.8] states "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone," which is the standard way commanders get cast (subject to the commander tax, {2} extra generic mana for each previous time it was cast from the command zone that game). If your commander card ends up in exile, [903.9a] gives you a state-based action: since it's a commander that was put into exile (or a graveyard) since state-based actions were last checked, its owner may move it into the command zone instead of leaving it in exile. In practice this means a commander that lands in exile is usually moved to the command zone rather than sitting there to be cast from exile.

That said, you CAN cast a commander from exile if some other rule or card effect specifically grants permission to cast it from exile. Rule [601.3f] makes clear that casting a spell always requires "a rule or effect [that] allows that player to cast it" from wherever it currently is. Examples of effects that grant this permission for a card in exile include: casting an Adventure spell, which leaves the card exiled and lets its controller cast it later as the creature (or original spell) per [715.3d]; a Plotted card, which its owner may cast from exile without paying its mana cost per [702.170d]; or any effect that lets you cast face-down exiled cards with certain qualities, per [406.3b]. If your commander qualifies under one of these (e.g., it has an Adventure or was plotted, or some other card grants exile-casting), you can cast it from exile using that permission — note [903.3d] confirms that being a commander is an attribute of the card itself that persists across zones, so a commander card cast from exile under such permission is still "casting a commander" for effects that care about that.

If you don't have such a specific enabling effect, the default answer is no — you'd instead use the state-based action in [903.9a] to put it into the command zone, then cast it from there under [903.8].

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer: During the cleanup step, four things happen, normally without any player getting priority: (1) If the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard down to that number — this is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1] [703.4n]. Damage that was lethal or would have destroyed a creature is cleared here too, but note that damage marked earlier still counts toward state-based destruction checks until this cleanup happens [120.6]. (3) Because this is a step in which no player normally receives priority, the cleanup step simply ends once these specified actions are completed — it doesn't wait for players to pass priority the normal way [500.3]. (4) However, there's an exception: after the discard and damage/effect removal, the game checks whether any state-based actions need to be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack (including abilities that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"). If either is true, those state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities go on the stack, and the active player gets priority so players can cast spells and activate abilities as normal; once the stack empties and everyone passes in succession, a whole new cleanup step begins. If nothing like that happens, no player gets priority and the cleanup step just ends [514.3] [514.3a] [704.3]. question: when can I concede a game?
answer: You can concede a Magic game at any time you choose — there's no restriction on timing. Rule [104.3a] states a player can concede at any time, and conceding causes that player to leave the game immediately and lose it. This applies even during another player's turn, in response to a spell, during a step that normally doesn't allow actions, etc., because rule [405.6g] confirms conceding doesn't use the stack and happens immediately whenever declared. Even if another player is controlling you (for example, due to a mind-control effect), that controller can't force you to concede, but you yourself may still concede at any time per rule [723.6]. Conceding is also the sole exception to card text overriding the rules: rule [101.1] specifies that no card can take away a player's right to concede at any time. In the Two-Headed Giant variant, if a player concedes, their entire team leaves the game immediately and that team loses, per rule [810.8b]. The rules provided don't give a different answer for standard multiplayer free-for-all beyond the general rule that the conceding player alone leaves and loses (per [104.3a]), so outside of Two-Headed Giant's team rule, conceding removes only that one player from the game.

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply the player whose turn it currently is. Rule [102.1] defines it directly: "A player is one of the people in the game. The active player is the player whose turn it is. The other players are nonactive players." So at any moment during a game, look at whose turn it is (i.e., who started the current turn and is progressing through its phases) - that person is the active player, and everyone else is a nonactive player.

This stays true even in special situations: if a player is being controlled by another player's effect during their own turn, rule [723.3] says that player is still considered the active player, even though someone else is making their decisions.

A few related points worth knowing:
- Being the active player matters a lot for priority: in most steps and phases the active player receives priority first (see rules [508.2], [509.2], [504.2], [507.2], [510.3], [505.6]).
- During the combat phase in a two-player game, the active player is also the attacking player, and the other player is the defending player ([506.2]). In a multiplayer game where opponents don't automatically all become defending players, the active player chooses one opponent to be the defending player ([507.1]).
- When multiple players must make choices at the same time, the active player chooses first, then the other players in turn order (the APNAP rule, [101.4] and [101.4e]).
- Some abilities specifically reference "the active player" as a single specific player, and the ability's controller picks which active player is meant if there's any ambiguity ([805.9]).
- If you're playing with the shared team turns option, it's actually the active team (the team whose turn it is) that matters most for these ordering rules, per [805.4a] and [805.6].

If you're playing a standard one-on-one or multiplayer game without special team-turn rules, the short version is: whoever's turn it currently is = the active player.

question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
answer:
Yes — as long as you had priority before casting the spell, you automatically get priority back afterward, and while that spell (or those spells) sit on the stack you may cast additional spells (or activate abilities) before anyone else gets a chance to act. This is what's commonly called 'holding priority.'

Rule [117.3c] states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward. Rule [601.2i] confirms the same for the specific act of casting a spell: once casting is complete, 'if the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority.' So after you finish casting Spell A, you get priority again immediately, and you can then cast Spell B in response to your own Spell A. Rule [117.7] confirms that a new spell cast while another is already on the stack is cast 'in response to' the earlier one and will resolve first (last-in, first-out stack order).

There is a timing restriction, though: instants can be cast 'any time' you have priority [117.1a], [304.1], but noninstant (sorcery-speed) spells can only be cast during your main phase while the stack is empty [117.1a]. So once you've cast one spell and it's sitting on the stack, the stack is no longer empty — you can keep holding priority to cast more instants (or activate abilities) in response, but you can't then cast a sorcery-speed spell until the stack empties again.

This works the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game — nothing in the priority rules given here differs by player count. The one exception in the provided rules is the Grand Melee multiplayer variant [807.5b], where there are multiple stacks (one per turn marker); there, if you have priority for more than one stack, you must specify which stack each new spell or ability goes onto, and it must follow the targeting/timing constraints tied to that stack. Outside of that specific variant, standard priority rules apply regardless of player count.

Note: rule [500.2] confirms that a phase or step only ends when the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, which is why holding priority to keep adding spells/abilities is possible before anyone else gets to respond.

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
answer:
A lore counter is put on each Saga you control (that has one or more chapter abilities) as a turn-based action immediately after your precombat main phase begins. This happens automatically and does not use the stack — it's not a triggered or activated ability that players can respond to before it happens.

Specifically: as the active player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga enchantment they control that has one or more chapter abilities [505.4] [703.4f] [714.3c]. This is a turn-based action, meaning it just happens as part of the phase beginning, with no opportunity for players to respond beforehand [714.3c]. Putting the lore counter(s) on may then cause one or more chapter abilities to trigger — a chapter symbol '{rN}—[Effect]' is a triggered ability that triggers 'When one or more lore counters are put onto this Saga, if the number of lore counters on it was less than N and became at least N' [107.15a] [714.2b]. Those triggered chapter abilities do go on the stack once they trigger, even though the placement of the counter itself does not.

Note that when a Saga first enters the battlefield, it gets its initial lore counter(s) not from this turn-based action but from a replacement effect tied to how it enters: a Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter on it, and a Saga with read ahead enters with a chosen number of lore counters (between 1 and its final chapter number) [714.3a] [714.3b] [702.155a] [702.155b] [614.1c]. After that, on each subsequent precombat main phase (starting with its controller's next one), the turn-based action adds another lore counter.

If a Saga's lore counters reach or exceed its final chapter number (and it isn't currently the source of a chapter ability still on the stack), its controller sacrifices it as a state-based action [714.4] [704.5s].

This rule applies the same way whether you're in a two-player or multiplayer game — it's simply tied to whoever the active player is and their own precombat main phase, regardless of how many players are at the table.

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect (from a resolving spell, a resolving ability, or a replacement effect being applied) that will do something later in the game rather than immediately, at the moment that effect is generated. It always contains the word "when," "whenever," or "at" somewhere in its text, even though that word usually won't be the very first word of the ability. Common examples are "exile this creature at the beginning of the next end step" or "when this creature becomes untapped, ..." — the triggering condition and effect are set up now, but the ability only actually triggers (and its effect only actually happens) at that later specified time or event.

Key points about how delayed triggered abilities work:
- They can be created by a resolving spell (source and controller = that spell and its controller as it resolved) [603.7d], by a resolving activated or triggered ability (source and controller = that ability's source and controller) [603.7e], by a static ability that generates a replacement effect (source/controller = the object with that static ability, at the time the replacement effect applied) [603.7f], or by a static ability that lets a player take an action (source/controller = the object with that static ability, at the time the action was taken) [603.7g].
- A delayed triggered ability won't trigger until it's actually been created, even if the event it cares about already happened just before it was created — if that makes the trigger event impossible, the ability simply never triggers [603.7a].
- Normally it triggers only once, the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it has a stated duration like "this turn"; if the event happens more than once simultaneously with no stated duration, its controller chooses which instance triggers it [603.7b].
- If it refers to a specific object, it still affects that object even if its characteristics change, but not if the object has left the zone it's expected to be in by the time the ability resolves (an object that left and returned is a new object under rule 400.7 and isn't affected) [603.7c].
- A special case called a "reflexive triggered ability" (rule 603.12) is a delayed triggered ability created mid-resolution of a spell/ability that lets or instructs a player to take an action, triggering on "when [a player] does/doesn't" that specific action taken during that resolution — it's checked immediately and only fires based on that particular instance of the action.

This is a general-rules concept (603.7 and 610.2), not tied to a two-player vs. multiplayer distinction — nothing in the provided rules suggests it works differently in multiplayer games.

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer: Yes. Instant and sorcery spells (non-permanent spells) can have abilities. Any text on an instant or sorcery spell counts as a "spell ability" — an ability that's followed as instructions while the spell resolves — unless that text is instead an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that meets the special criteria in rule 113.6 [113.3a]. So a non-permanent spell's abilities aren't limited to just spell abilities; it can also carry activated, triggered, or (in limited cases) static abilities, though rule 113.6 notes that abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that spell is on the stack, with certain stated exceptions [113.6]. More generally, an ability is one of the characteristics an object can have that lets it affect the game, and abilities generate effects when the object resolves or is activated/triggers [113.1a][113.2d].

question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
answer:
Yes. Split Second only prevents players from casting spells or activating abilities that aren't mana abilities while the split-second spell is on the stack — mana abilities are explicitly excluded from that restriction. Rule [702.61a] defines split second as: "As long as this spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities." Rule [702.61b] confirms this directly: "Players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack. Triggered abilities trigger and are put on the stack as normal while a spell with split second is on the stack."

This works because mana abilities are a special category of ability under [113.4] and [605.1] — they don't use the stack and can be activated whenever a player has priority or is in the middle of paying a cost, per [605.3a]. Since they never go on the stack ([605.3b]), split second's restriction (which is about casting spells and activating non-mana abilities) simply doesn't apply to them. Triggered mana abilities work the same way and resolve immediately without using the stack ([605.4a]).

This is true whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game — the split second rule and the mana ability exception aren't dependent on player count.
